foundations.title: Biomechanics Fundamentals
foundations.summary: How forces act on the human body during movement.

sections.title: Force, torque, and moment arms
content: Force is any interaction that changes motion or posture in the body.
In human movement, forces originate from muscles, gravity, and external loads.
Torque is rotational force produced around a joint when force is applied at a distance.
Moment arms determine how much torque a muscle or load produces.
Small changes in joint position can dramatically increase muscular demand and joint stress.
Understanding torque explains why some positions feel easy while others feel unstable or heavy.

sections.title: Joint loading principles
content: Joint loading describes how forces are transmitted through joints during movement.
Efficient movement distributes load across muscles and joints rather than concentrating stress.
Poor mechanics can increase compressive or shear forces beyond tissue tolerance.
Repeated excessive loading is a primary contributor to overuse injuries.
Healthy joints adapt to progressive load when movement quality is maintained.

sections.title: Efficiency vs compensation
content: Efficient movement uses the most appropriate joints and muscles for a task.
Compensation occurs when the body avoids a weak, painful, or restricted area.
Short-term compensation may preserve performance under fatigue or injury.
Long-term compensation often leads to overload in secondary tissues.
Identifying compensation patterns is key to injury prevention and performance longevity.

foundations.title: Human Anatomy Overview
foundations.summary: Key structures involved in movement and performance.

sections.title: Bones and joints
content: Bones provide structural support and act as levers for movement.
Joint shape determines available range of motion and stability.
Some joints prioritize mobility while others prioritize stability.
Joint alignment affects how forces are transmitted through the body.
Poor alignment increases stress on cartilage, ligaments, and tendons.
Healthy joints rely on both structure and muscular control.

sections.title: Muscle roles
content: Muscles generate force by contracting and pulling on bones.
Prime movers create the main motion during an exercise.
Stabilizers control joint position and prevent unwanted movement.
Synergists assist prime movers to improve efficiency.
Poor coordination between muscle roles reduces performance.
Balanced recruitment protects joints and improves power output.

sections.title: Connective tissue
content: Connective tissues include tendons, ligaments, and fascia.
Tendons transmit force from muscle to bone.
Ligaments provide passive joint stability.
Fascia helps distribute force across regions of the body.
Connective tissue adapts slowly compared to muscle.
Gradual loading is essential to maintain tissue health and resilience.

foundations.title: Movement Patterns
foundations.summary: Foundational human movement categories that underpin strength, performance, and injury resilience.

content: The squat is a foundational lower-body movement pattern used in daily life and sport.
Efficient squatting distributes force across the hips, knees, and ankles rather than overloading one joint.
Depth should be determined by mobility, control, and intent rather than arbitrary standards.
Loss of balance, knee collapse, or excessive forward lean often signal strength or mobility limitations.
Mastery of the squat builds a base for jumping, running, and lifting performance.
sections.title: Squat

content: The hinge pattern emphasizes hip flexion with a relatively stable spine.
Proper hinging loads the posterior chain, including the glutes and hamstrings.
Spinal movement during hinges often indicates compensation or insufficient hip control.
Deadlifts, kettlebell swings, and hip thrusts are common hinge variations.
A strong hinge pattern protects the spine during lifting and daily tasks.
sections.title: Hinge

content: Push patterns involve force production away from the body using the upper extremities.
Efficient pushing depends on coordinated scapular movement and shoulder stability.
Poor pushing mechanics often lead to shoulder irritation or neck tension.
Push-ups, presses, and overhead movements all rely on push pattern fundamentals.
Balanced push development supports performance and injury resilience.
sections.title: Push

content: Pull patterns counterbalance pushing movements and support shoulder health.
Strong pulling improves posture by reinforcing scapular retraction and control.
Rows, pull-ups, and carries all express pull mechanics differently.
Weak pulling patterns often contribute to rounded shoulders and neck strain.
Pull strength is essential for both athletic performance and longevity.
sections.title: Pull

content: Rotation patterns transfer force between the lower and upper body.
Effective rotation originates from the hips and trunk rather than the spine alone.
Uncontrolled rotation increases stress on the lumbar spine.
Anti-rotation strength is just as important as rotational power.
Rotational control enhances agility, throwing, and change-of-direction ability.

sections.name: Setup and stance

sections.title: Fundamentals
content: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Initiate motion from the hips rather than the lower back.
Keep the load close to the body to reduce spinal stress.
Drive through the hips to return to standing.
Control the descent to maintain positional awareness.

sections.title: Fundamentals
content: Keep the torso tall and stable during the movement.
Track the front knee in line with the toes.
Control depth to maintain balance and joint alignment.
Push evenly through the front foot to return.
Avoid excessive forward lean or collapse.

sections.title: Fundamentals
content: Maintain shoulder stability during pressing motions.
Control scapular movement rather than locking the shoulders.
Brace the core to support force transfer.
Avoid flaring elbows excessively under load.
Move smoothly through the full range of motion.

sections.title: Fundamentals
content: Initiate pulling from the upper back rather than the arms.
Maintain neutral spine posture throughout the movement.
Control the return phase to avoid momentum.
Keep shoulder blades coordinated and stable.
Avoid shrugging or excessive neck tension.
